title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
description: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.The region's G
body: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire. It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

schema.headline: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg

title: Student who spells by blinking is denied chance to sit exam
description: Tracey Campbell, of Rett UK, said Romi had been dismissed in many areas of her life and she wanted to prove she was capable."To have these extra barri
body: Tracey Campbell, of Rett UK, said Romi had been dismissed in many areas of her life and she wanted to prove she was capable."To have these extra barriers put in place is completely unfair and unjust," she said."What has been fabulous about exam boards in England is that people have been allowed to sit their exams over a long period of time, one question at a time."Glasgow Clyde College, where Romi studies, said she is "highly capable and committed".Claire Donaghey, assistant principal arts and continuing education, said: "Despite considerable discussion with Qualifications Scotland, the mitigating arrangements we have proposed have not been deemed compatible with these requirements."We remain fully committed to supporting Romi and will continue to work constructively with her, her family and Qualifications Scotland to explore every available option and achieve the best possible outcome for her."Qualifications Scotland said it was committed to making reasonable adjustments so that disabled learners have an equal opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge, skills and understanding. A spokesperson said: "This year over 39,000 learners benefited from assessment arrangements. "We also have a duty to maintain the integrity of qualifications, so must always ensure that any reasonable adjustments put in place for learners do not impact standards."

schema.headline: Student who spells by blinking is denied chance to sit exam

title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
description: Image source, FacebookImage caption, Ian Haggis - pictured when he was younger - died when the light aircraft crashed near Loch LomondByClaire Diamond
body: Image source, FacebookImage caption, Ian Haggis - pictured when he was younger - died when the light aircraft crashed near Loch LomondByClaire DiamondBBC ScotlandUpdated 3 hours agoAn 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis. He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released. The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene. Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.A road near the scene of the crash remains closed, with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.Tributes posted on social media by former students describe the flying instructor as "a gentleman and an experienced aviator", and a "good friend". The plane - a Piper Tomahawk II aircraft - is registered to Leading Edge Flight Training in Renfrew, according to the Civil Aviation Authority's aircraft register., external Previous social media posts on Leading Edge's Facebook page report the instructor's nickname as the 'Flying Haggis', and show that he had been working with the flying school. BBC Scotland has approached Leading Edge Flight Training for comment.Image caption, Police remained at the scene on Sunday and blocked off Old Drymen Road near the crash Gavin Birch-Williams, managing director of Glasgow Airport, said: "We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow Airport."This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow Airport are with the friends and families affected."The plane had earlier taken off from Cumbernauld Airport at 11:46, before flying 15 minutes to Glasgow Airport.It stayed there until about 13:00, before doing a two-hour flight north east to Newport-on-Tay then turning round and heading back to Glasgow.It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and started its final flight.

schema.headline: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named

title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper
description: The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.Yvette Cooper told the BBC the
body: The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in a hospital corridor in 2024.The health secretary has announced £140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised. Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029. "That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards." The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade. Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients. On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after spending the final hours of his life in an A&E corridor in north London was highlighted.Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor. "He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor." The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened extended their condolences to the family.They said they continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors. "Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions," they said.On Friday health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN), also expressed their concern over corridor care, writing a letter to the health secretary urging her to take action.It said the practice was fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.This weekend Cooper announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from.It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying earlir this month there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.Swords said there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year. RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point"."The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.

schema.headline: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper

title: I lost my hair to chemo - now my wigs are worn by A-list stars
description: Antonia says she saw a gap in the market when she was surrounded by "terrible" wigs while working in TV and film, including in the ITV series Bad Girl
body: Antonia says she saw a gap in the market when she was surrounded by "terrible" wigs while working in TV and film, including in the ITV series Bad Girls two decades ago."Women wanted natural-looking wigs and they just weren't available. They looked like helmets!"Antonia set up a Facebook page and began advertising on Gumtree. "I had very limited resources. I didn't have any investors behind me. I come from very humble beginnings."Her experience dealing with MS has helped her success, she says. Antonia lost her hair when she underwent chemotherapy following a bone marrow transplant, so she knows what it is like to be "completely bald".This made her relate more deeply to her customers, she explains, as she understands the loss of control some women feel when they lose their hair."I didn't feel like myself," she says, "but being able to put on a wig that looks something close to how your hair was, or the look you used to have, it's as though you can feel like yourself again."When she sees a woman put a wig on and her "whole face lights up", it can be "very, very rewarding"."When we feel good about ourselves...we're more confident, we can achieve more. I felt like I was changing the world, one person at a time."While Antonia's business, A-List Lace Hair, has grown from strength to strength, with salons in London and New York, she has been dealing with the impact of her health conditions.She struggles with fatigue due to her MS and uses a wheelchair, but says this has not stopped her success. Instead, it has simply changed the way she has run her business."I used to feel that being a good entrepreneur was being able to do as much as I can myself," Antonia said. "Due to my health challenges, there are days where I literally can't feel my legs, they feel like jelly, there's days where I'm completely exhausted after sleeping, I wake up completely shattered." This has forced her to "trust other people and gain strength in building a team".As a woman in business, being in a wheelchair can sometimes make Antonia feel "smaller" as people often have to look down at her at industry events. "People are often surprised when I start speaking about my business, as though they're thinking 'how have you accomplished all of this in a wheelchair?'"Antonia, who has three young children, says that being underestimated can be a good thing, and she wants to remain open about her health to inspire other women.She says she used to feel "weak" because of her disability, but now feels she has gained "so much strength" from sharing her experience online.Asked what she would say to another woman who may fear her age, disability or health could get in the way of success, she says: "I would encourage them to just start.""You might not have control over your health, you might not know what tomorrow is going to bring, and you might not have all the resources. But start with what you do have, and let's see what could happen next."

schema.headline: I lost my hair to chemo - now my wigs are worn by A-list stars

title: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley arena in one turbulent year
description: A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the follo
body: A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night.As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers.The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya Pınar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal Yelekçi and main dancer Esin Bahat.But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions."After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal Yelekçi, playing on the group's name.manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 Türkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group.They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including Gülçin Ergül, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show.The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify.While in London, they released their first English-language single, TRALALA, which topped YouTube's daily music video chart on its release, ahead of videos from Shakira and Taylor Swift.The music video was also their first to be filmed outside Turkey, with the group working with a largely British production crew in east London."Getting out from that safe zone was a bit stressful for us," says Pınar.Despite their hopes to perform on British and American stages, they're keen to retain their Turkish identity."We want to reach a global audience with our Turkish songs actually, not with English ones," says Sude Oktay."We want to teach people to sing in Turkish."Alongside Turkish girl group Hepsi, manifest cite the Spice Girls among their musical inspirations.Pınar says her favourite Spice Girl is Baby Spice."Because of the pink. I'm pink and blonde, so it's obvious," she laughs.They have also had the chance to meet one of the world's biggest pop stars, Dua Lipa. The British-Albanian singer met manifest backstage before watching them perform at her Sunny Hill Festival in Kosovo in July this year."She came to our backstage and said a lot of great things," one member recalls."We really love her, her songs, her stage presence."On the day of the concert, there was a sense of excitement outside Wembley Arena as fans wearing manifest-branded headbands and carrying banners gathered.The crowd was predominantly Turkish women in their 20s and 30s, many dressed in colours associated with the group. Among them were friends Elif, 31, and Zeynep, 25, both Turkish women living in London, who reflected on the band's past year."I don't think I've ever heard of a girl band performing there," says Zeynep."I think I was seven when Hepsi were last together. It's maybe a once-in-a-lifetime experience."Turkish pop star Tarkan previously performed at Wembley Arena in 2008.For Elif, the concert has a wider significance."We are going through difficult times back home. It means girl power and empowerment, and just having fun and being together," she says."I feel like back home people came together to support them and criticise the treatment that they were receiving from the government."Zeynep adds: "It's great to see them here, but I hope one day they will be back in Turkey and they'll be able to do whatever they want without getting persecuted for it."

schema.headline: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley arena in one turbulent year

title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting in Nottingham city centre
description: Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are
body: Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family, and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire Police," she added.​"Nottingham City Council is working tirelessly alongside the police to support the investigation and ensure those responsible are swiftly caught and brought to justice.​"While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, our commitment to keeping Nottingham safe is absolute. "Thanks to the daily bravery of our police and community protection officers, Nottingham remains a safe city, and residents can be assured that every available resource is being deployed."In a post on social media, Nadia Whittome, MP for Nottingham East, encouraged anyone with information to contact the police. "My thoughts are with the injured police officer and his family following this truly shocking incident," she wrote. "We all wish him a full and speedy recovery."

schema.headline: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting in Nottingham city centre

title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper
description: NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the heal
body: NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who have breached NHS data and privacy standards.Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately. Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff. "Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS.Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff" and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.NUH added a new system, currently under testing, is being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

schema.headline: NHS data breaches a disgrace, says Health Secretary Yvette Cooper

title: Leeds vs Man Utd player ratings: Dominic Calvert-Lewin denies Man Utd - who rated highest?
description: Leeds United XI:James Trafford: Brave enough to race 30 yards out of his box to clear when failure to execute would have been disastrous. Leeds defend
body: Leeds United XI:James Trafford: Brave enough to race 30 yards out of his box to clear when failure to execute would have been disastrous. Leeds defenders know they can give him the ball under pressure. 7James Justin: Swung over a couple of early crosses to test the visitors' defence but caught on his heels by Mbeumo for Man Utd goal. 6Nico Elvedi: Near-post header almost put Leeds in front. 7Tarik Muharemovic: Calm in possession but visitors' set-up left him with no-one to mark at times. Major threat at the other end though, with header setting up Calvert-Lewin equaliser. 7Jayden Bogle: An attacking threat from wing-back as Leeds pushed forward and had shot saved by Lammens. 7Ethan Ampadu: Lucky to get away with no card for a late tackle on Mbeumo at start. Usual assured display. 6Ao Tanaka (off 79, Longstaff): Maybe a little too cautious at times. Got into the game as Leeds pressed after leveller. Long-range effort over. 6Gabriel Gudmundsson: Caught Andrey Santos from behind and was booked. Did really well to force Amad back when the Ivorian wanted to run free on goal. 7Anton Stach: Wasn't able to control midfield duels in opening period but second half was better. 6Noah Okofor (off 72, Nmecha): No chance to repeat Old Trafford heroics. Lashed a second-half shot over and poor pass when he might have released Calvert-Lewin. 6Dominic Calvert-Lewin: Grew into the game after subdued start. One first-half header wide, another straight at Lammens in second. Strong enough to control and apply finish to level. 8Subs:Lukas Nmecha (on 72, Okafor): Worked hard to try and create. 5Sean Longstaff (on 79, Tanaka): 6Subs not used: Zetterer, Wilson, Aaronson, Bijol, Bahoya, Bard, Gruev.Man Utd XI:Senne Lammens: Good save to deny Elvedi and solid performance. 7Leny Yoro: Given a stern physical test despite starting at right-back. Thrown in at the deep end this season. 6Harry Maguire: Another largely solid display. Came out on top in one-to-one duel with Calvert-Lewin in first half but found it much harder in the second. 7Lisandro Martinez (off 46, Mazraoui): Kept his place despite inflammatory comments and was cheered by Man Utd fans, booed by Leeds'. Did well enough. Replaced at the break. 6Diogo Dalot: Yet another different left-back option. Held his own but he shouldn't really be in that position. 6Andrey Santos: Another industrious performance which questioned why he had been used so sparingly previously. 7Carlos Baleba: Keen to get on the ball and carry it forward. Partnership with Santos brings energy. He even tried a 25-yard shot but it was off target. 7Amad Diallo: Pace was a threat, even if visitors didn't make most of it. Second-half shot blocked. 6Youri Tielemans: Excellent cross for Mbeumo opener. More effective with two midfielders behind him. 7Bruno Fernandes: Overhit a free-kick in a dangerous position and sent it out for a throw, then booked for late tackle on Muharemovic. Everything seems forced and a struggle at the moment. 6Bryan Mbeumo: Started in an inside left position and tried to link play but not a natural role. Should have scored with first-half header, didn't threaten with another opportunity but persevered and eventually got his goal. Not strong enough to hold Calvert-Lewin off for equaliser. 7Subs:Noussair Mazraoui (on 46, Martinez): Leeds more of a threat when he came on. Vital injury-time block. 6 Mason Mount (on 72, Baleba): Can be effective and tried to create but limited impact. 6Matheus Cunha (on 84, Tielemans): 6Subs not used: Darlow, De Ligt, Rashford, Zirkzee, Lacey, Amass.

schema.headline: Leeds vs Man Utd player ratings: Dominic Calvert-Lewin denies Man Utd - who rated highest?

title: Green Party leader Zack Polanski says he will not overturn Zionism motion
description: Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.The Green leader told Sunday
body: Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation. Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it."At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner. "I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel. "One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.Asked if he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said did not think this was controversial, adding: "I think what's controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years."Kuenssberg asked Polanski if he accepted that for many Jewish people, Zionism was the right to have a safe place to live, or homeland."I think that's what people think it means, but actually in practical application - which is what we're talking about here - that homeland has come to the cost of the Palestinian people," Polanski, who is Jewish, said."I want equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - the practical application of Zionism has not resulted in that."When questioned if he thought Israel had a right to exist, he said he did not think "any state has a right to exist under international law".And asked if he would apologise for his handling of the row, as the Jewish Greens chair Vivien Lichtenstein has asked him to do, Polanski said: "I'm not sorry at all."In response, the Board of Deputies president Phil Rosenberg accused Polanski of being "all over the place" on the issue."Let us remember that, as of now, the Green Party's platform erases Jewish identity and experience, calls for Israel's elimination, and tells the vast majority of Jews, who overwhelmingly believe in the right of Israel to exist, that they are not welcome in the party," Rosenberg added.Polanski has said no Jewish Green members will be excluded based on their faith or background - and that being Jewish and supporting Israel are "two separate things".His latest comments come after a fortnight of criticism from across the political spectrum over the motion.Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it "antisemitic". Polanski said it was up to Green councillors to do what they saw fit.

schema.headline: Green Party leader Zack Polanski says he will not overturn Zionism motion

title: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions
description: Making murder fun: How the Traitors' soundtrack sets the toneFigure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic co
body: Making murder fun: How the Traitors' soundtrack sets the toneFigure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic correspondentSuspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning."I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach."They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."Image source, Sam WattsImage caption, Sam Watts' Traitors theme helped to establish the show's identityFor the title sequence, the 44-year-old wanted something memorable. As a kid, his favourite song was Bernard Hoffer's gloriously over-the-top Thundercats theme, external, so that's the level he aspired to."I was trying to write something that signified the show was starting, so that people would run in from making their cup of tea in the kitchen to watch it."And I wanted a memorable melody that people could hum, because it helps with the identity of the show."The Traitors theme is "one of the biggest pieces of music I've ever written", he says, recorded with a full orchestra and overdubbed with dozens of electronic elements to create a heightened, hyperreal atmosphere.That bled into the 20 or so other pieces Watts wrote, which also appear in dozens of international spin-offs.The idea, he says, is that the whole hour feels like a film trailer, with viewers permanently waiting for the psychological pressure chamber to explode.To achieve that, he employed several techniques of trailer music - most notably the "Braam", a klaxon-like punctuation mark invented for Christopher Nolan's Inception (see video for a fuller exploration).Show producer Sarah Fay took that concept and amplified it. "We wanted to just supersize it and make it feel like a drama, not like your usual reality [show]," she said in a rare interview with Metro, external when the first civilian series aired in 2022."We wanted to make it feel like that edge-of-your-seat cinematic drama with, you know, elements of Succession, and we wanted it to feel like Knives Out when you get into the castle!"To achieve that, she commissioned additional music from film trailer composers, including Hans Zimmer's company Bleeding Fingers. But she also sprinkled in a handful of creepy cover versions.Some became instant classics - such as a sinister spin on Britney Spears' Toxic, external, or a version of Tears For Fears' Mad World, external seemingly broadcast on a tannoy from Hades.They're so integral to The Traitors' aesthetic that it might surprise you to learn they weren't recorded specifically for the show.Image caption, The Traitors score has proved so popular that an entire BBC Proms concert was devoted to the show's music last yearBoth examples were created by German writer-producers 2wei.Based in Hamburg, they had no idea their music had appeared in The Traitors until friends in the UK messaged them in excitement."We were just flipping out," says 2wei's Simon Heeger. "It's completely different to how we ever thought it would be used."Heeger founded 2wei, pronounced "zwei", in 2016 with his old college friend Christian Vorländer.They had both spent time in LA working on advertisements and (stop me if you're sensing a theme here) film trailers, before moving home to build a music production empire."Christian worked on the Mad Max soundtrack, which is really known for the big drums and the orchestral scale – and that was really the starting point of our sound," says Heeger."Whenever you hear big epic drums with an orchestral sound and maybe a female vocal on top of it, it's usually something we had our fingers in."Image source, 2weiImage caption, Simon Heeger is the co-founder of 2wei, which is responsible for some of Traitors' most memorable cover songsTheir big break came with a stormy reworking of Destiny's Child's Survivor, which featured in the trailer to Alicia Vikander's Tomb Raider, external.Since then, their music has appeared in films like Wonder Woman and video games such as League of Legends. In The Traitors, original 2wei songs like Blindside, external now feature alongside their covers (other producers, including SYML and Damned Anthem also contribute songs to the show).Heeger says their background in commercials makes the music perfectly suited to the show's slippery skullduggery."In adverts, you only have a few seconds to convey a certain emotion and, especially in Traitors, where there are cliffhangers and moments that you don't expect, you need music that comes to the point right away but still has a boldness to it."It's a sweet spot, and it's not easy to convey, but every now and then it works quite well."Fans agree. On Spotify, there are hundreds of playlists dedicated to the programme's background music. Some are tailored to murder mystery parties and Halloween events. Others compile more sedate moments under labels like "gentle tension" or "chill elder emo watching Traitors".But never forget: the soundtrack is playing a deceitful game of its own."A lot of my music has a wink in it and, for The Traitors, it's a little silly and slightly over the top," says Watts."I think it helps the nastier side of things - the murder, the plotting - feel a bit more fun."

schema.headline: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions

title: France protests: Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
description: France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bike
body: France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris. Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful.They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings. Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas. In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons."It's like we had a war," Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told news agency AFP. Another resident, Anita GrasIt, said it was "terrifying" to see groups of young people "smashing everything, with total impunity".The looters were "proudly carrying supermarket baskets filled with goods and laughing about their thefts", Maryse, a woman living nearby who gave only her first name, told the BBC. Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille, a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted.More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured in the unrest on Saturday, France's interior ministry said.Around 1,500 shops and retailers were also damaged in the disturbances, the Retail and Trade Federation said. On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the aftermath, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace. Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris. Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich."The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la République which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor. The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process. The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations. Close to the Place de la République, a BBC reporter visited the Good Vibes bakery, whose glass front was completely shattered, and the Nicolas wine store, where every bottle was either stolen or smashed, leaving smell of alcohol lingering in the street. CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves.Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police. Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said. In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost.""A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department. Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media."Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said.

This comes after he said he ‘wasn’t a big fan’ of Volodymyr Zelensky. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian president at a summit in Brussels said the Europeans were ‘real leaders’.
Laura is joined by BBC world affairs editor John Simpson to discuss why the US president is becoming more friendly with Russian President Vladimir Putin. 
Plus, John marks 60 years at the BBC by sharing his most memorable moments from his career reporting around the world.
